DEPARTMENT 731 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 21STCV05404    Hearing Date: June 30, 2026    Dept: 731

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

 

DEPARTMENT 731

 

TENTATIVE RULING

 

B&S VENTURERS, INC., a California Corporation; BARJOR SOLI PITHAWALLA, an individual,

 

                                  Plaintiffs,

 

         v.

 

AMGUARD INSURANCE COPMANY; CARMEN MARTINEZ, an individual, and DOES 1 to 50, inclusive

 

                                  Defendants.

 

 Case No:  21STCV05404

 

 

 

 

 

 Hearing Date:  June 30, 2026

 Calendar Number:  1

 

 

 

           Plaintiff B&S Ventures, Inc. moves to compel Defendant AmGuard Insurance Company to serve further responses to Special Interrogatories (Set Three) Nos. 75 to 78, and Request for Production of Documents (Set Three) Nos. 78, 80, 84, 86, 88, and 89 pursuant to the Court’s discovery order on December 17, 2025. The plaintiff also moves for sanctions of $4,345 against the defendant.

 

           The motion is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART as follows.

 

           The request to compel further responses is GRANTED as to Estimating Supervisor Corey Massaro’s estimates under the defendant’s Estimate Review Team’s 2020 guidelines. The defendant is ordered to produce the relevant documents, information, and/or compilation of data within 60 days of this ruling.

 

The request to compel further responses is otherwise denied.

 

           The request for sanctions is denied.

 

Background

 

This is an insurance action. Plaintiffs B&S Ventures, Inc. (“BSV”) and Barjor Soli Pithawalla (collectively, “Plaintiffs”) allege that, after Defendant Carmen Martinez (“Martinez”) negligently drove her car through their Harbor City restaurant on or about September 12, 2019, they submitted a timely insurance claim to their insurer, Defendant AmGuard Insurance Company (“AmGuard”), but Defendant unreasonably delayed the handling, adjustment, and resolution of their claim.

 

On February 10, 2021, Plaintiffs filed their Complaint against AmGuard, Martinez, and Does 1 to 50, inclusive, asserting causes of action for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and negligence.

 

On September 28, 2023, Plaintiffs dismissed Martinez.

 

On September 11, 2025, BSV filed motions to compel AmGuard’s further responses to Requests for Production of Documents, Set Three, and Special Interrogatories, Set Three.

 

On December 17, 2025, the Court granted BSV’s motions in part, ordering AmGuard to serve further responses to certain interrogatories and requests for production within 60 days (the “December 17 Ruling”).

 

On May 20, 2026, BSV filed the instant motion to compel AmGuard’s compliance with the December 17 Ruling, arguing that the defendant has failed to produce all responsive documents and withheld responsive information in violation of the order.

 

On June 16, 2026, AmGuard filed its opposition.

 

BSV filed its reply on June 23, 2026,

 

Jury trial is set for November 2, 2026.

 

Legal Standard

 

“On receipt of a response to a demand for inspection, copying, testing, or sampling, the demanding party may move for an order compelling further response to the demand if the demanding party deems that … [a] statement of compliance with the demand is incomplete[;] … [a] representation of inability to comply is inadequate, incomplete, or evasive[; or] … [a]n objection in the response is without merit or too general.”¿ (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.310, subd. (a).)

Similarly, “[o]n receipt of a response to interrogatories, the propounding party may move for an order compelling a further response if the propounding party deems that any of the following apply: ¶ (1) An answer to a particular interrogatory is evasive or incomplete. ¶ (2) An exercise of the option to produce documents under Section 2030.230 is unwarranted or the required specification of those documents is inadequate. ¶ (3) An objection to an interrogatory is without merit or too general.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.300, subd. (a).)

 

If the motions are granted and the responding party fails to provide the discovery responses, the court may impose monetary sanctions against that party. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2030.300, subd. (e); 2031.310, subd. (i); see also id. §§ 2023.010, subd. (g) [stating that misuse of the discovery process includes disobeying a court order to provide discovery responses]; 2023.030, subd. (a) [stating that courts may impose monetary sanctions for misuse of the discovery process if such sanctions are authorized by a discovery statute].)

          

Discussion

           Before considering the merits of the motion, the Court reviews the Plaintiffs’ allegations and the case’s procedural history in greater detail to better understand the parties’ positions and the relevance of the discovery in dispute.

           In support of BSV’s May 2025 motion to compel production of documents and reopen discovery, BSV’s counsel attested to the following facts.

During the deposition of the defendant’s Person Most Knowledge, Mark Burns (“Burns”), on May 6, 2025, BSV “learned for the first time that AmGUARD utilizes an internal unit, known as the Estimate Review Team, that reviews building property estimates submitted to AmGUARD during the handling and adjustment of an insurance claim. [BSV] further discovered that the Estimate Review Team operates under a set of written policies, procedures, and guidelines that are separate and apart from the AmGUARD claims handling policies, procedures, and guidelines previously produced by AmGUARD [during discovery].” (Declaration of Lindsey Downey, Esq., filed May 15, 2025, in support of (“ISO”) Motion to (1) Compel Defendant to Produce Documents, and (2) Reopen Discovery for a Limited Purposes (“Downey Decl. ISO Reopen Discovery Motion”), ¶ 3.)

Plaintiffs also learned through subsequent discovery “that Corey Massaro [“Massaro”], was an Estimating Supervisor at AmGUARD’s Estimate Review Team, and was directly involved in the adjustment of Plaintiff’s claim.” (Downey Decl. ISO Reopen Discovery Motion, ¶ 5.)

“Mr. Massaro reviewed repair estimates prepared by Defendant’s retained independent building consultant, John Machin of Young & Associates, and instructed Mr. Machin to remove various items from the estimate. Mr. Massaro also approved a figure for tenant improvements and betterments [for Plaintiffs’ restaurant] that was lower than all submitted estimates—including Mr. Machin’s revised estimate, which had been adjusted in accordance with Mr. Massaro’s directive.” (Downey Decl. ISO Reopen Discovery Motion, ¶ 5.) “While Plaintiff was previously aware of Mr. Massaro’s role in the claim, Plaintiff did not know until the May 6, 2025 PMK deposition that he was part of the Estimate Review Team and that the team operated under a separate set of internal standards distinct from the claims handling materials previously produced by AmGUARD in discovery.” (Id. at ¶ 7.)

           In its motion to compel production of documents and reopen discovery, BSV argued that it “will be severely prejudiced if denied the opportunity to obtain documents and conduct limited discovery about AmGUARD’s Estimate Review Team as this information [was] highly relevant to Plaintiff’s claims of bad faith and punitive damages being asserted against AmGUARD in the instant action.” (Downey Decl. ISO Reopen Discovery Motion, ¶ 15.)

           On June 12, 2025, the Court held the hearing on and granted BSV’s opposed motion to compel production of documents and reopen discovery, stating in relevant part:

“In the RFPs [i.e., Requests for Production] at issue, BSV requested document relating to AmGuard’s policies and procedures, investigation, and adjustment relating to Plaintiff’s claims. AmGuard produced no documents regarding the Estimate Review Team. AmGuard contends that this position is justified because BSV’s RFPs did not request information about the Estimate Review Team by name. The Court disagrees. Documents regarding the Estimate Review Team’s policies and procedures are necessarily relevant if it was involved in evaluating BSV’s claim.” (6/12/25 Minute Order, pp. 4-5.)

“[In addition, the motion to reopen discovery is granted because] … BSV promptly sought discovery after learning of the Estimate Review Team’s existence. Further, there is evidence suggesting that the Estimate Review Team, including Massaro, played a key role in the eventual decision on BSV’s claim. BSV would be prejudiced if it were forced to go to trial without more complete information on the Estimate Review Team.” (6/12/25 Minute Order, p. 5.)

           Subsequently, on September 11, 2025, BSV filed the underlying motions to compel AmGuard’s further responses to Requests for Production of Documents, Set Three (“RFPs”), Nos. 75-89, 92, 95 and 96, and Special Interrogatories, Set Three (“SROGs”), Nos. 60-64, 68-72, and 74-78. AmGuard opposed both motions.

           After the hearing on those motions on December 17, 2025, the Court issued the December 17 Ruling, stating as follows in relevant part:

Afte[r] reviewing all moving papers and considering all oral arguments, the Court rules as follows.

The Court orders that defendant produce further responses and responsive documents to the following discovery requests within 60 days. The parties are encouraged to meet and confer about the trial date.

The Court limits the discovery responses to (1) work by the estimate review team under the 2020 guidelines, which will include work for the years until the guidelines changed; (2) shall not include full claim files; and (3) shall not necessarily include portions of claim files unless there is a further meet and confer between the parties.

The Court makes this order with respect to the following discovery requests:

Interrogatories 60, 61, 74, 75, 76, 77, and 78.

Requests for Production 75, 76, 78, 80, 84, 86, 88, 89, 92, 95 and 96.

(12/17/25 Minute Order, p. 1.)

           Plaintiff now moves to compel AmGuard’s compliance with the December 17 Ruling, arguing that AmGuard violated the order by failing to provide all responsive documents or information concerning the following SROGs and RFPs.

·       SROG 75: What percent of ESTIMATES for commercial property damage claims that were reviewed by YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM, from 2018 to the present, were reduced in value and/or scope—whether in whole or in part—of the original estimate?

·       SROG 76: What percent of ESTIMATES for commercial property damage claims that were reviewed by YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM, from 2018 to the present, were increased in value and/or scope—whether in whole or in part—of the original estimate?

·       SROG 77: What percent of ESTIMATES for commercial property damage claims that were reviewed by Corey Massaro, in connection with his role on YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM, from 2018 to the present, were reduced in value and/or scope—whether in whole or in part—of the original estimate?

·       SROG 78: What percent of ESTIMATES for commercial property damage claims that were reviewed by Corey Massaro, in connection with his role on YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM, from 2018 to the present, were increased in value and/or scope—whether in whole or in part—of the original estimate?

·       RFP 78: All DOCUMENTS and COMMUNICATIONS that evidence, reflect, or relate to the total number of commercial property damage claim ESTIMATES, from 2018 to the present, in which YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM reduced the value and/or scope—whether in whole or in part— of the original estimate.  

·       RFP 80: All DOCUMENTS and COMMUNICATIONS that evidence, reflect, or relate to the number of ESTIMATES for commercial property damage claims, from 2018 to the present, that were increased—whether in value and/or scope, in whole or in part—by YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM.  

·       RFP 84: All DOCUMENTS and COMMUNICATIONS that evidence, reflect, or relate to the number of ESTIMATES for commercial property damage claims, from 2018 to the present, that Corey Massaro reduced—whether in value and/or scope, in whole or in part—in connection with his role on YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM.  

·       RFP 86:   All DOCUMENTS and COMMUNICATIONS that evidence, reflect, or relate to the number of ESTIMATES for commercial property damage claims, from 2018 to the present, that Corey Massaro increased—whether in value and/or scope, in whole or in part—in connection with his role on YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM.

·       RFP 88: All DOCUMENTS and COMMUNICATIONS evidencing the total dollar amount of ESTIMATES submitted to YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM for commercial property damage claims, for each year from 2018 to present.

·       RFP 89: All DOCUMENTS and COMMUNICATIONS evidencing the total dollar amount deducted by YOUR ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM from ESTIMATES relating to commercial property damage claims, from each year from 2018 to the present.

(Separate Statement, filed May 20, 2026, pp. 3:11-28, 8:8-9:8.) The discovery requests defined “ESTIMATES” as “any and all repair and/or scope estimates relating to commercial property losses submitted to [Amguard], from 2018 to the present, that were reviewed by the ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM.” (Id. p. 2:25-27.) They also defined “ESTIMATE REVIEW TEAM” as “the department and/or group of individuals identified by [Amguard’s] person most knowledgeable, Mark Burns during his depositions in the subject action.” (Id. at p. 3:1-3.)

           BSV’s counsel testifies that AmGuard did not provide all documents and information requested by those SROGs and RFPs and, consequently, failed to comply with the December 17 Ruling for the following reasons. “In its responses, AmGuard states that approximately 7,900 claims were submitted to the Estimate Review Team. [However,] [t]he Xactanalysis report that AmGuard refers to in its responses to the subject discovery contains data pertaining to only 1,846 claims submitted to the Estimate Review Team. [Therefore], data from over 6,000 claims is missing from the Xactanalysis report, and none of the data in the Xactanalysis report pertains to estimates reviewed by Corey Massaro.” (Declaration of Attorney William A. Foster, filed May 20, 2026, ¶ 9.)

After reviewing the parties’ papers, the Court finds that AmGuard did not violate the December 17 Ruling.

Rather, the parties’ dispute arose out of their different interpretations of the ruling. BSV believed that the Court required AmGuard to produce all responsive documents and information subject to certain limitations. On the other hand, defense counsel interpreted BSV’s counsel’s comments at the hearing to mean that BSV was only seeking production of the Xactanalysis report. (See Declaration of Wynn C. Kaneshiro, ¶ 29 [“[A]t the December 17, 2025 hearing, BSV’s counsel reiterated that it was not interested in other insureds’ claim file materials but rather wanted aggregate date on estimates. BSV’s counsel argued that AmGUARD can generate reports using Xactanalysis that would have the aggregate information on estimates”]; id. at ¶ 31 [“In compliance with the Order, AmGUARD served supplemental responses to the interrogatories and document requests identified in the Order and produced additional documents including the Xactanalysis Report that BSV requested at the hearing”].) The December 17 Ruling does not support any of the parties positions as it neither mentions or limits discovery to the Xactanalysis report nor does it require AmGuard to produce data from all 7,900 claims that were submitted to its Estimate Review Team. (The Law Firm of Fox & Fox v. Chase Bank, N.A. (2023) 95 Cal.App.5th 182, 203 [“The same rules apply in ascertaining the meaning of a court order or judgment as in ascertaining the meaning of any other writing [e.g., a contract].’ [Citations]”]; Civ. Code, § 1638 [“The language of a contract is to govern its interpretation, if the language is clear and explicit, and does not involve an absurdity”].)

           Therefore, BSV’s argument that AmGuard violated the December 17 Ruling is unpersuasive.

           Nevertheless, the Court has established in prior rulings that the SROGs and RFPs seek information relevant to Plaintiff’s claims. Indeed, the Complaint alleges, among other things, that AmGuard breached its duty of good faith and fair dealing towards Plaintiffs by, among other things: “Ignoring estimates prepared by its own consultants that identified the scope and value of certain aspects of the property loss as more than AmGuard had initially contended, and instead undertaking efforts designed to minimize the value of Plaintiffs’ claim[.]” (Compl., ¶ 85(K).) The Complaint also alleges that AmGuard violated several provisions of subdivision (h) of Insurance Code section 790.03. (Compl., ¶¶ 88, 106.) That statute “prohibits insurers from ‘knowingly committing or performing with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice’ a variety of ‘unfair claim settlement practices.’” (Colonial Life & Accident Ins. Co. v. Superior Court (1982) 31 Cal.3d 785, 790 (Colonial Life) [italics removed].) In Colonial Life, the California supreme court held that the discovery of the names, addresses, and files of other insurance claimants with whom a defendant insurer adjuster attempted settlements was relevant to the subject matter of the action and could lead to admissible evidence regarding “the frequency of alleged unfair settlement practices …,” and “the elements for punitive damages [which] may be suggested by a pattern unfair practices.” (Id. at pp. 791-792.) 

Therefore, the question remains whether AmGuard should be compelled to produce documents and/or information from data that could not be included in its Xactanalysis report.

           Burns, Amguard’s PMK, testifies that generating a similar report for the remaining 6,054 claims would be onerous and cost the company approximately $587,238 for the following reasons. “In order to provide information on the 6,054 claims submitted from March 1, 2020 to June 22, 2022 that are not located on the Xactanalysis platform,  AmGUARD would have to review the claim file to locate the original estimate, any subsequent estimates, determine the value of the estimates, the amount of reductions or increases and the rationale for any changes, if any, and attribute actions to individual team members (e.g., Corey Massaro), which may require cross-referencing internal communications and audit logs. Many files contain unstructured data (e.g., adjuster notes, email threads, scanned documents in claim files) that cannot be queried automatically. Determining whether an estimate was ‘reduced’ or ‘increased’ often requires subjective interpretation of file notes and supporting documentation. Additional technical resources may be needed to assist with data extraction, spreadsheet compilation, and validation. This review will take an average of 2.5 hours per file or 15,135 hours for the 6,054 claims. At the hourly rate of $38.80 per hour, it will cost $587,238 to conduct the review. It will take over 378 weeks or over 7 years for one person to complete the review. Notably, additional hours will be required to locate the responsive documents from each claim file to respond to the document demand.” (Burns Decl., filed June 16, 2026, ¶ 19.)

           However, Burns has admitted that “[n]one of the estimates reviewed by Corey Massaro from March 2020 to July 30, 2021 [the end date of Massaro’s employment with Amguard] are on the Xactanalysis platform.” (Burns Decl., filed June 16, 2026, ¶¶ 13, 14.) The Court agrees with BSV that, at a minimum, it is entitled “to the documents and data concerning the estimates by Corey Massaro ….” (Reply, p. 4:1-2.) BSV alleges that Massaro was directly involved in the adjustment of Plaintiffs’ insurance claim. Therefore, data concerning his estimates are relevant to this action.

           AmGuard has not argued that compiling data from Massaro’s estimates alone would be unduly burdensome. Rather, its estimates have been from all remaining 6,054 claims that were submitted to the Estimate Review Team regardless of whether Massaro was involved. There is no evidence that compiling a report from Massaro’s estimates would be as expensive as it would have been for the company to do so for all remaining claims.

           Therefore, the Court grants BSV’s request to compel AmGuard’s further responses to the SROGs and RFPs at issue. The production shall be narrowed to Massaro’s estimates and “under the 2020 guidelines” as previously limited by the December 17 Ruling.

Notwithstanding the above ruling, monetary
sanctions against AmGuard would be unjust given the Court’s finding above that
the discovery dispute arose from the parties’ different interpretations of what
the December 17 Ruling required. As the ruling did not support either party’s
interpretation, AmGuard did not engage in the misuse of the discovery process. 

           BSV’s request for sanctions is DENIED.


Case Number: 23SSTCV02342    Hearing Date: June 30, 2026    Dept: 731

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

 

DEPARTMENT 731

 

TENTATIVE RULING

 

GEORGE ANDRAOS  

 

                                  Plaintiff, 

   

         v. 

 

 

LIFETIME HOME BUILDERS, INC., et al., 

 

                                  Defendants. 

 

 Case No:   23STCV02342

 

 

 

 

 

 Hearing Date:  June 30, 2026

 Calendar Number:  2

 

           

Defendant Lifetime Builders, Inc. moves to compel Plaintiff George Andraos’ responses to Form Interrogatories, Special Interrogatories, Requests for Production of Document, and to Deem Requests for Admissions Admitted.

 

Defendant’s motions are DENIED as moot on the condition the responses are provided before the hearing on this motion. In the event that Plaintiff has not provided responses before the hearing, Defendant shall inform the Court and the motions will be granted.

 

Defendant’s request for sanctions is GRANTED. Plaintiff is ordered to pay Defendant sanctions in the amount of $2,580 within 20 days of this order.

 

Background

 

This is an action for breach of the contract. On February 2, 2023, Plaintiff George Andraos (“Plaintiff”) filed a complaint against Defendants Lifetime Home Builders, Inc., Altisource Solutions, Inc., dba Granite Risk Management, alleging causes of action for breach of contract, intentional misrepresentation and negligence. 

Plaintiff alleges that commencing in or about August 2, 2019, Plaintiff and Defendant entered into a written agreement for Defendants to provide certain home improvement services to Plaintiff’s residence. Defendants performed most of these services below industry and trade standards and not in a workmanlike quality.

On May 13, 2026, Defendant Lifetime Builders, Inc. (“Defendant”) filed these motions to compel Plaintiff’s responses to Form Interrogatories, Special Interrogatories, and Request for Production of Documents.

On May 14, 2026, Defendant filed this motion to Deem Requests for Admissions Admitted.

 

On June 11, 2026, Plaintiff filed an Opposition.

 

On June 18, 2026, Defendant filed a Reply.

 

Legal Standard

Compel Interrogatories

 

            If a party to whom interrogatories are directed fails to serve a timely response, the propounding party may move for an order compelling responses and for a monetary sanction.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.290, subd. (b).) The statute contains no time limit for a motion to compel where no responses have been served. All that need be shown in the moving papers is that a set of interrogatories was properly served on the opposing party, that the time to respond has expired, and that no response of any kind has been served.  (Leach v. Superior Court (1980) 111 Cal.App.3d 902, 905–906.)

 

Deem RFAs Admitted 

 

“If a party to whom requests for admission are directed fails to serve a timely response, the following rules apply: The requesting party may move for an order that the genuineness of any documents and the truth of any matters specified in the requests be deemed admitted…. (Code Civ. Proc. § 2033.280(b).) The Court, on motion, may relieve that party from this waiver on its determination that both of the following conditions are satisfied: (1) The party has subsequently served a response that is in substantial compliance with Sections 2033.210, 2033.220, and 2033.230. (2) the party’s failure to serve a timely response was the result of mistake, inadvertence, or excusable neglect…. (Code Civ. Proc. § 2033.280(a).) The court shall make this order, unless it finds that the party to whom the requests for admission have been directed has served, before the hearing on the motion, a proposed response to the requests for admission that is in substantial compliance with Section 2033.220. (Code Civ. Proc. § 2033.280(c).)

 

Compel RPDs 

 

Where there has been no timely response to a demand for the production of documents, the demanding party may seek an order compelling a response.  (Code Civ. Proc. § 2031.300(b).)  Failure to timely respond waives all objections, including privilege and work product.  (Code Civ. Proc. § 2031.300(a).)  Thus, unless the party to whom the demand was directed obtains relief from waiver, he or she cannot raise objections to the documents demanded.  There is no deadline for a motion to compel responses.  Likewise, for failure to respond, the moving party need not attempt to resolve the matter outside court before filing the motion. 

 

            Sanctions

 

Sanctions are mandatory in connection with a motion to deem matters specified in a request for admissions as true. Sanctions are also mandatory in connection with motions to compel responses to interrogatories and requests for production of documents against any party, person, or attorney who unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion to compel unless the court “finds that the one subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.”  (Code Civ. Proc. §§ 2030.290(c), 2031.300(c), 2033.280(c).) 

Discussion

On February 11, 2026, Defendant served Form Interrogatories, Special Interrogatories, Request for Productions, and Request for Admissions, Sets One, on Plaintiff. (Weinberg Decl., Exh. 1.) Responses were due by March 16, 2026. (Id.) Despite several extensions, Plaintiff has failed to provide responses.

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that responses will be provided before the hearing.

As such, the motions are denied as moot on the condition that Plaintiff provides the responses before the hearing on this motion. In the event that Plaintiff fails to provide responses prior to the hearing, Defendant shall inform the Court, and the motions will be granted.

Defendant seeks sanctions against Plaintiff. While Plaintiff asks that the Court deny the request for sanctions, Plaintiff fails to provide any justification for the failure to provide timely responses. Further, sanctions in connection with a motion to deem requests for admissions are mandatory with no exception. As such, Defendant’s request for sanctions is granted.

            Defendant seeks sanctions in the amount of $3,284.75 for the motion to compel responses to form interrogatories, $584.75 for the motion to compel responses to special interrogatories, $1,284.75 for the motion to compel responses to request for production, and $1,284.75 for the motion to deem requests for admissions admitted.

 

            Defendant’s request for sanctions is reduced due to the simplicity of the motions and the nature of the concurrent facts. Thus, Plaintiff is ordered to pay Defendant sanctions in the amount of $2,580 ($400 per hour for 6 hours, plus $180 filing fees), within 20 days of this order.


Case Number: 23STCV27927    Hearing Date: June 30, 2026    Dept: 731

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

 

DEPARTMENT 731

 

TENTATIVE RULING

 

PARVANEH SAFAEI,

 

                                  Plaintiff,

 

         v.

 

 

THE BOEING CO., et al.

 

                                  Defendants.

 

 Case No:  23STCV27927

 

 

 

 

 

 Hearing Date:  June 30, 2026

 Calendar Number:  3

 

 

Defendant The Boeing Co. moves for a protective order imposing certain restrictions on depositions noticed by Plaintiff Parvaneh Safaei. The defendant also moves for sanctions of $30,000 against the plaintiff’s counsel based on the latter’s conduct during prior depositions.

 

Code of Civil Procedure section 2025.420, subdivision (g) states: “If the motion

for a protective order is denied in whole or in part, the court may order that the deponent provide or permit the discovery against which protection was sought on those terms and conditions that are just.”

 

Pursuant to that statute, the motion is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART as follows.

 

The request for a protective order requiring both parties’ counsel to turn on their cameras while questioning witnesses during video depositions is GRANTED.

 

The Court also orders counsel for both parties to act civilly during depositions, to avoid and/or keep repeated questions to a reasonable minimum, and to refrain from inquiring into matters outside the scope of their clients’ respective deposition notices.

 

The motion is otherwise DENIED.

 

Background

 

           This is an employment discrimination case.

 

           The Complaint alleges that, while working for Defendant The Boeing Co. (“Boeing”) as a software engineer, Plaintiff Parvaneh Safaei (“Plaintiff”) was diagnosed with cancer and underwent surgeries that left her with physical limitations. After she returned to work, her supervisor for years was replaced by Defendant Benjamin Canfield (“Canfield”), who repeatedly discriminated, harassed, and retaliated against her because of her limitations, requests for reasonable accommodations, Iranian national origin, age, and/or taking care of her elderly, disabled mother. Canfield subsequently terminated Plaintiff under false accusations of timecard fraud.

 

           On November 14, 2023, Plaintiff filed this action against Boeing, Canfield, and Does 1 through 100, inclusive, asserting causes of action for: (1) discrimination based on actual or perceived disabilities and/or serious medical condition; (2) discrimination based on actual or perceived associational disabilities; (3) failure to engage; (4) failure to accommodate; (5) discrimination based on national origin; (6) discrimination based on age; (7) retaliation based on actual or perceived participation in protected activities; (8) harassment and/or hostile work environment; and (9) failure to prevent.

 

           On April 27, 2026, Plaintiff filed a motion to compel one of Boeing’s Person Most Qualified (“PMQ”), Sue Ellen Wallace, to appear for the “second volume” of her deposition. Boeing opposed the motion.

 

           On May 7, 2026, Boeing filed the instant Motion for Protective Order.  

 

On June 16, 2026, the Court denied Plaintiff’s motion to compel, finding that: (1) contrary to Plaintiff’s argument, the Civil Discovery Act allows Boeing to move for protective order before, during, or after a deposition; and (2) it was unnecessary to grant Plaintiff’s request to compel the PMQ deposition at the time because the Court will still need to rule on Boeing’s motion for a protective order against the deposition.

 

           Plaintiff filed her opposition to Boeing’s motion on June 16, 2026.

 

           On June 30, 2026, Boeing filed its reply.

 

           Jury trial is set for March 22, 2027.

          

Legal Standard

 

           “Before, during, or after a deposition, any party, any deponent, or any other affected natural person or organization may promptly move for a protective order. The motion shall be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under Section 2016.040.” (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2025.210, subd. (b); 2016.040 [“A meet and confer declaration in support of a motion shall state facts showing a reasonable and good faith attempt, either in person, by telephone, or by videoconference, to informally resolve each issue presented by the motion”].)

 

“The court, for good cause shown, may make any order that justice requires to protect any party, deponent, or other natural person or organization from unwarranted annoyance, embarrassment, or oppression, or undue burden and expense.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.420, subd. (b).) “This protective order may include, but is not limited to, one or more of the following directions: ¶ (1) That the deposition not be taken at all. ¶ …. ¶ …. ¶ …. ¶ (5) That the deposition be taken only on certain specified terms and conditions. ¶ …. ¶ …. ¶ (8) That the testimony be recorded in a manner different from that specified in the deposition notice. ¶ (9) That certain matters not be inquired into. ¶ (10) That the scope of the examination be limited to certain matters.” (Ibid.)

 

Discussion

Boeing moves for a protective order imposing the following restrictions on Plaintiff’s depositions of defense witnesses: (1) prohibit Plaintiff from continuing PMK depositions of witnesses who have already been deposed, and from taking PMK depositions on topics already covered; (2) require opposing counsel to activate his camera during questioning at remote depositions; and (3) require counsel to provide the deponent with full, usable copies of all exhibits used during questioning. (Notice of Motion, p. 3:8-26.) Boeing also moves for an order appointing a discovery referee and imposing sanctions of $30,000 “against Plaintiff’s counsel, including attorneys’ fees and the cost of a discovery referee.” (Id. at pp. 4:27-4:9.)

The Court finds that Boeing has satisfied the meet and confer requirement for this motion. (Declaration of Melanie Renken, filed May 7, 2026 (“Renken Decl.”), ¶¶ 12-25.)

A.    Plaintiff’s Request to Prohibit Additional PMK Depositions and Deposition of Topics Already Covered

According to defense counsel, Boeing has produced to date three PMQs for depositions, Matt Wilson (“Wilson”), Sue Wallace (“Wallace”), and Kathryn Lewis (“Lewis”), and each PMQ was designated to testify on different topics from the others.

Boeing has produced Wilson for Volume I and II depositions, but has refused to produce Wallace and Lewis for the second volume of their depositions until the Court rules on this motion. (Renken Decl., ¶¶ 5-7, 10, 20, 21, 24.)

Boeing argues that the Court should prohibit Plaintiff from taking additional PMQ depositions for three reasons. (Motion, pp. 15:19-17:7 [providing the reasons].) First, Plaintiff’s counsel spent hours revisiting topics previously covered, and the duplication extended across witnesses. Second, Plaintiff’s counsel spent an inordinate amount of time questioning PMQ witnesses outside the scope of the topics in the deposition notices. Third, additional PMQ depositions would only serve to harass Boeing and its witnesses.

1.     Accusation of Revisiting Topics Previously Covered

Boeing argues that during Wilson’s deposition, Plaintiff’s counsel duplicated several topics. The Court evaluates each of those allegations, in turn as shown in the table below.

Topics

Allegedly Duplicated

Wilson Vol. I

(Renken Decl., Exh. C, begins on page 207 of the PDF) Transcript Citations

Wilson Vol. II

(Renken Decl., Exh. N, begins on page 623 of the PDF)

Transcript

Citations

 

The Court’s Findings

Investigator qualifications

 

82:15-91:7

 

381:24-383:10

 

The Court disagrees that Vol. II questioning on this topic was unnecessary. As Plaintiff’s counsel explained the cited portion of Vol. II, Wilson referred counsel to job descriptions but in Vol. II the deponent went into more details regarding qualifications.

Investigations identified as “potentially significant” (and whether Plaintiff’s investigation was identified as such)

 

124:24-145:8; 175:4-

177:21

Plaintiff has also failed to show Vol. II questioning was unnecessary for this topic. The Vol. II questioning at issue mainly focused on a document that, during Vol. I, Plaintiff’s counsel claimed (and defense counsel did not dispute) had not been produced. The document was allegedly produced before Vol. II deposition.

Plaintiff’s knowledge of the evidence and purpose of the investigation

 

159:8-166:6

The Court finds that Plaintiff’s counsel repeated some questions in Vol. II that he had already asked in Vol. I. Specifically, questions regarding (a) whether the relevant investigator would have told Plaintiff the “precise accusations” that were being made against her and gave her the opportunity to respond, and (b) if the best practice would be for an investigator to tell the accused what the specific accusations are.

 

However, the portion of the Vol. II transcript that Boeing has highlighted also went into more details that were not covered in Vol. I. Specifically, in Vol. II, Plaintiff’s counsel asked Wilson whether he had reviewed records that suggested the relevant investigator informed Plaintiff of what she is being investigated of.

 

Therefore, while it was improper for counsel to repeat questions already asked and answered on that topic, Boeing has not shown that Vol. II was unnecessary.

94:10-96:10, 185:12-

189:4

The Court finds that Plaintiff’s counsel repeated in Vol. II a Vol. I question regarding Boeing’s quality review. Specifically, counsel asked Wilson to testify define once again what a quality review was.

 

However, the line of questioning that followed shows that counsel was seeking clarification regarding Wilson’s testimony regarding that topic.

 

Therefore, Plaintiff has not shown the quality review topic in Vol. II was unnecessary.

The Court does not find the questioning in Vol. II was a duplicate of the questions asked in Vol. I. While both Plaintiff’s counsel asked Wilson regarding credibility assessments in both depositions, Vol. II deposition concerned whether the investigator at issue could determine the credibility of witnesses through phone investigations. In the portion of the Vol. I transcript that Plaintiff has cited, Plaintiff’s counsel did not ask Wilson regarding credibility assessments during phone investigations.

The Court finds that Plaintiff’s counsel asked Wilson in Vol. I and II the same questions: who is April Newman and Leslie Peterson and what were their roles. However, during Vol. II, after Wilson protested that counsel had already asked him a repeated question regarding Leslie Peterson, counsel acknowledged, stating: “Yeah, I know. I - - she’s listed here. I’m just curious why.” (Vol. II, p. 508:3-4.)

 

Boeing also argues that the duplication extended across witnesses because Plaintiff’s counsel questioned both Wilson and Wallace about Boeing’s “PRO-784 reasonable accommodation process” and investigator training, topics that were designated for different PMQ witnesses. (Motion, p. 15:26-28.)

However, Boeing has not cited which part of Wilson’s transcripts it is referring to. Therefore, the Court disregards that argument as to Wilson.

As for the PRO-784 argument regarding Wallace, Boeing contradicts itself, stating that Wallace was designated to testify regarding PRO-784. (Motion, p. 12:5-11.)

With regard to the accusation that Plaintiff’s counsel questioned Wallace on investigator training, the Court disagrees with Boeing. Plaintiff’s counsel asked the PMQ a question that was within the purview of topics in the PMQ’s Volume I deposition notice. (See Renken Decl., ¶ 7; Exh. D – a copy of the Wallace Vol. I Deposition Notice, pp. 1:25-2:19 [seeking to depose Wallace on the following topics: “(1) the essential and marginal duties of Plaintiff’s job during the five year period preceding the termination of Plaintiff’s employment; ¶ (2) every occasion defendant came upon information indicating Plaintiff’s need for reasonable accommodations during Plaintiff’s employment; ¶ (3) every time defendant engaged Plaintiff’s in the interactive process to identify all available reasonable accommodations during Plaintiff’s employment; ¶ (4) every accommodation considered for, offered to and/or furnished to Plaintiff during plaintiff’s employment; and (5) every policy and procedure defendant had in place during Plaintiff’s employment for engaging disabled employees in the interactive process and offering available reasonable accommodations” (capitalized letters removed)]; see also Motion, p. 12:16, citing Exh. E – a copy of the Vol. I Wallace deposition transcript, p. 93:19-94:2 [asking Wallace a question within those topics she was designated: “Q Okay. Were the generalists, the HR generalists at Boeing to your knowledge trained on California requirements regarding the accommodations of disabled employees? ¶ A MR. LOVELL: Calls for speculation, outside the scope. ¶ Q BY MR. BAKHTIAR: You can answer. ¶ A I don’t have access to what the training requirements are for HR generalists in California”].))

In all, the Court finds that Plaintiff’s counsel did not engage in the kind of extreme duplication suggested by Boeing.

2.     Accusation of Spending an Inordinate Amount of Time Questioning on Matters Outside the Scope of Topics in Deposition Notices

Boeing argues that Plaintiff’s counsel spent “substantial time questioning PMK witnesses about topics outside the scope of their notices. For example, Wilson was questioned about Boeing’s disciplinary process and reasonable accommodations—neither of which was included in his investigation-focused PMK notice. (Wilson Vol. I, 233:4–237:22; Wilson Vol. II, 485:11–17[.]) Wallace was asked to interpret California disability law and opine on Boeing’s compliance with the Fair Employment and Housing Act [“FEHA”]—subjects well outside her accommodations designation. (Wallace Dep. 87:13–88:8; 100:17–102:18; 130:9–137:24.) Lewis was questioned about control account managers and their job responsibilities, which had nothing to do with her termination and performance management designation. (Lewis Dep. 104:19–108:15.) Each hour spent on out-of scope questioning was an hour unavailable for the noticed topics—and is now cited by Plaintiff as a basis for additional deposition time.” (Motion, p. 16:5-15.)

The Court has reviewed the cited portions of the deposition transcripts.

The Court disagrees with Boeing that Wilson was improperly questioned regarding Boeing’s disciplinary process and reasonable accommodations. The line of questioning fell within the “investigation-focused PMK notice.” (Renken Decl., Exhs. B, G – copies of Vol. I & II Deposition Notices of Wilson.)

The Court agrees with Boeing that it was improper for Plaintiff’s counsel to keep asking Wallace questions regarding Boeing’s interpretation of FEHA statutes. That line of questioning requested legal conclusions from the witness, which was not only improper but unnecessary, as Plaintiff can propound requests for admissions instead. (Renken Decl., Exh. D – a copy of Wallace’s Vol. I Deposition Notice; Exh. E – copy of the Wallace deposition transcript.)

The Court also agrees with Boeing that, during Volume I deposition of PMQ Lewis, it was improper for Plaintiff’s counsel to keep questioning the PMQ regarding Boeing’s control account managers’ duties, as that was outside the scope of the deposition notice. (See Renken Decl., ¶ 11 [testifying that Lewis was designated to testify regarding the following topics: “(1) the termination of Plaintiff’s employment, including each and every reason for the termination; (2) every person who participated in and/or was involved in the decision to terminate Plaintiff’s employment; and (3) every performance management policy and procedure Defendant had in effect during the ten-year period preceding the termination of Plaintiff’s employment, including Defendant’s disciplinary policies and procedures and termination policies and procedures”]; id. at Exh. I – a copy of the Lewis Vol. I Deposition Notice.) In her opposition, Plaintiff does not explain why she deposed the PMQ on that topic.

3.     Accusation that Additional Depositions Will Only Harass Boeing and Its Witnesses

Boeing argues that the Court should enter a protective order prohibiting additional PMQ depositions and restricting Plaintiff from taking PMQ depositions on topics already covered for the reasons discussed above.

The defendant also argues: “Plaintiff had ample opportunity during the nearly seven hours spent questioning each witness to explore the noticed categories. Instead, Plaintiff chose to waste substantial time on unnoticed topics, legal quizzes, and argument. Having squandered that time, Plaintiff should not be permitted to subject Boeing’s witnesses to additional depositions to cover the same ground. The Court should therefore prohibit further PMK depositions of witnesses who have already testified and bar additional depositions on topics already covered.” (Motion, pp. 16:24-17:3 [footnote removed].)

However, as Plaintiff argues in its opposition, “[g]enerally, a deponent seeking a protective order will be required to show that the burden, expense, or intrusiveness involved in the videotaped deposition clearly outweighs the likelihood that the information sought will lead to the discovery of admissible evidence.” (Emerson Electric Co. v. Superior Court (1997) 16 Cal.4th 1101, 1110; Opposition, pp. 13:26-14:3.)

Here, Boeing has not shown that Plaintiff’s counsel’s conduct during PMQ depositions outweighs the likelihood that Plaintiff will obtain admissible evidence. Indeed, in its motion, Boeing concedes that the seven-hour limitation on deposition testimony in Code of Civil Procedure section 2025.290, subdivision (a) does not apply to employment cases. (Motion, p. 16, fn. 10.)

Therefore, Boeing’s request for an order prohibiting Plaintiff from taking additional PMQ depositions and preventing Plaintiff’s counsel from asking questions regarding topics previously noticed is DENIED. Instead, the Court shall enter an order requiring both parties’ counsel to act civilly during the depositions, avoid and/or keep repeated questions at a reasonable minimum, and refrain from inquiring into matters outside the scope of their respective deposition notices.

B.    Request for an Order Requiring Opposing Counsel to Activate His Camera During Remote, Video Depositions

Boeing also moves for a protective order requiring opposing counsel to activate his camera during questioning at remote depositions, arguing that Code of Civil Procedure section 2025.420, subdivision (h) protects witnesses from unwarranted annoyance, embarrassment, or oppression. (Motion, p. 17:9-14.) Boeing further argues that if Plaintiff’s counsel does not want to be on camera, California Rules of Court, rule 3.1010(a) permits telephone depositions. (Id. at p. 17:15-16.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that there is no law requiring counsel to be on camera. (Opposition, p. 15:7-18 [arguing that in Agnone v. Agnone (2025) 111 Cal.App.5th 758, 766-767, the California Court of Appeal affirmed a trial court’s order imposing nearly $10,000 in sanctions against a defense attorney that refused to turn on his camera while seating in the same room as the witness preventing the deposing attorney from being able to see whether the defense attorney was coaching the deponent. Plaintiff argues case is inapplicable here because the questioning attorney is the one off camera].)

The Court finds that to the extent Plaintiff asked the witnesses to appear on a Zoom or other video deposition, her counsel should be prepared to also appear on camera. It is a matter of professional courtesy to the witnesses, court reporter, and opposing party. Otherwise, the depositions can take place through phone.

Therefore, Boeing’s request for a protective order requiring counsel to turn on their cameras during video depositions is GRANTED. In so ruling, the Court is not preventing the parties stipulating otherwise in future depositions.

C.    Request for an Order Requiring Counsel to Provide the Deponent With Full, Usable Copies of All Exhibits Used During Questioning

Boeing also argues: “Mr. Bakhtiar insists on questioning witnesses about multi-page documents while sharing only a narrow, zoomed-in portion of a document. (Wilson Vol. II, 295:22–24; 317:25-319:17). In response to defense counsel’s objections and request that Wilson be provided with the full documents about which he was being questioned, Mr. Bakhtiar threatened to require Wilson to travel from his home in St. Louis, Missouri to California if he wanted to see the exhibits in their entirety.” (Motion, pp. 17:21-18:4.) “A witness cannot fairly testify about a document they cannot see in full.” (Id. at p. 18:6-7.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that screen-sharing of exhibits during remote deposition is standard practice and there is no law supporting Boeing’s request. (Opposition, p. 17:5-10.) In addition, that “[t]he Court should not issue an order dictating the logistics of a remote deposition when the parties have shown they can handle them cooperatively.” (Id. at p. 17:14-15.) In this case, “[t]he Wilson Volume II transcript shows that defense counsel and Plaintiff’s counsel actively addressed exhibit-handling on the record, including Ms. Renken’s own suggestion that Plaintiff’s counsel share the HAIL report (Wilson Vol. II, 295:22–24) and her offer to email a document to the witness (Wilson Vol. II, 318:7–9, 319:14–17).” (Id. at p. 17:10-13.)

The Court DENIES Boeing’s request. Without knowing how voluminous each exhibit will be, issuing a blanket order requiring sharing the full pages of the exhibits may only work to delay the depositions. The parties’ counsel may continue screen-sharing relevant portions of exhibits as long as the witnesses are given the opportunity to review the entire document upon request from the witness or opposing counsel. Counsel can continue to discuss on record how to share exhibits during depositions.

D. Request for discovery referee

Code of Civil Procedure section 639 (“Section 639”) states: “When the parties do not consent [to the appointment of a referee], the court may, upon … its own motion, appoint a referee in the following cases pursuant to the provisions of subdivision (b) of Section 640: ¶ …. ¶ …. ¶  …. ¶ …. ¶ (5) When the court in any pending action determines that it is necessary for the court to appoint a referee to hear and determine any and all discovery motions and disputes relevant to discovery in the action and to report findings and make a recommendation thereon.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 639, subd. (a).)

However, as Plaintiff argues, Section 639 requires the referee appointment to be based on “exceptional circumstances.” (See Code Civ. Proc., § 639, subd. (a)(2) [“When the referee is appointed pursuant to paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) [i.e., for discovery purposes], [the court shall indicate in its written order appointing the referee] the exceptional circumstances requiring the reference, which must be specific to the circumstances of the particular case”]; Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.920, subd. (c) [“A discovery referee must not be appointed under Code of Civil Procedure section 639(a)(5) unless the exceptional circumstances of the particular case require the appointment”].)

No California case has defined what Section 639 means by “exceptional circumstances.”

The California Court of Appeal has suggested, however, that simplistic cases involving “run-of-the-mill” (i.e., ordinary) discovery disputes do not constitute exceptional circumstances. (See Hood v. Superior Court (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 446, 449, fn. 4 [“Moreover, the order made in this case purports to refer ‘any and all’ future discovery disputes to the appointed referee. Whatever merit there may be to the notion of a reference of all discovery disputes in a complex case with a history of nasty nit-picking and name-calling, there is nothing about this case to justify its placement in that category. It is one thing to refer out a particularly complex discovery dispute that appears to involve an extraordinary expenditure of judicial time. It is quite another to refer out all discovery, however simplistic, in a routine tort action such as this—where there appears to be no legitimate reason for the court to refuse to hear and decide run-of-the-mill discovery motions”]; see also Taggares v. Superior Court (1998) 62 Cal.App.4th 94, 104 [noting that “there is no suggestion the Legislature intended [the court’s] powers [under Section 639] to be used over the parties’ objection in routine, pro forma, uncomplicated matters simply for expediency or a distaste for discovery resolution”].)

Boeing has not shown exceptional circumstances here.

Therefore, the request to appoint a referee is DENIED.

E.    Request for monetary sanctions of $30,000 against Plaintiff’s counsel

“The court shall impose a monetary sanction under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 2023.010) against any party, person, or attorney who unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion for a protective order, unless it finds that the one subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.420, subd. (h).)

 

The Court finds that Plaintiff’s counsel acted with substantial justification in opposing the instant motion. Indeed, the Court has rejected most of Boeing’s characterization of counsel’s conduct during the depositions at issue.

 

Therefore, the request for monetary sanctions of $30,000 against Plaintiff’s counsel is DENIED.


Case Number: 24STCV19691    Hearing Date: June 30, 2026    Dept: 731

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA 

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES 

 

DEPARTMENT 731

 

TENTATIVE RULING 

 

TERESA L. BALLEK,  

 

                                  Plaintiff, 

   

         v. 

 

 

FORD MOTOR COMPANY, et al., 

 

                                  Defendants. 

  

 Case No:  24STCV19691

 

 

 

  

 

 Hearing Date:  June 30, 2026 

 Calendar Number:  5

 

Defendants Ford Motor Company and Sunrise Ford of North Hollywood move for summary judgment or in the alternative, summary adjudication as to Plaintiff Teresa L. Ballek’s Complaint.

Defendants’ motion for summary judgment, or in the alternative, summary adjudication is DENIED in part and GRANTED in part. It is denied as to causes of action 1-4 and granted as to the fifth cause of action for negligent repair.

Background 

This is an action for lemon law. On August 6, 2024, Plaintiff Teresa L. Ballek (“Plaintiff”) filed a complaint against Defendants Ford Motor Company (“Ford”) and Sunrise Ford of North Hollywood (“Sunrise Ford”; together, “Defendants”), alleging causes of action for: (1) Violation of subdivision (d) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (2) Violation of subdivision (b) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (3) Violation of subdivision (a)(3) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (4) breach of the implied warranty of merchantability; and (5) negligent repair (against Sunrise Ford).

The complaint alleges that on or about December 28, 2023 (the Court notes Defendant’s MSJ states the date is December 28, 2022), Plaintiff entered into a warranty contract with Defendant Ford regarding a 2023 Ford Maverick. Plaintiff alleges the vehicle developed defects including transmission defects, engine defects, and electrical defects, and that Defendant Ford has been unable to service or repair the vehicle to conform it to the applicable express warranties after a reasonable number of opportunities.

On December 24, 2025, Defendants filed this motion for summary judgment, or in the alternative, summary adjudication. On June 10, 2026, Plaintiff filed an Opposition. On June 17, 2026, Defendants filed a Reply.

Legal Standard 

 

The purpose of a motion for summary judgment or summary adjudication “is to provide courts with a mechanism to cut through the parties’ pleadings in order to determine whether, despite their allegations, trial is in fact necessary to resolve their dispute.” (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co., supra, 25 Cal.4th at p. 843.) In analyzing such motions, courts must apply a three-step analysis: “(1) identify the issues framed by the pleadings; (2) determine whether the moving party has negated the opponent's claims; and (3) determine whether the opposition has demonstrated the existence of a triable, material factual issue.”¿(Hinesley¿v.¿Oakshade¿Town Center¿(2005) 135 Cal.App.4th 289, 294).¿ “Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivision (c), requires the trial judge to grant summary judgment if all the evidence submitted, and ‘all inferences reasonably deducible from the evidence’ and uncontradicted by other inferences or evidence, show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” (Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp. (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119.)¿ 

 

“In ruling on the motion, the court must consider all of the evidence and all of the inferences reasonably drawn therefrom [citation] and must view such evidence [citations] and such inferences [citations] in the light most favorable to the opposing party.” (Aguilar, supra, at pp. 844-845 [quotation marks omitted].)¿ 

 

“On a motion for summary judgment, the initial burden is always on the moving party to make a prima facie showing that there are no triable issues of material fact.” (Scalf v. D. B. Log Homes, Inc. (2005) 128 Cal.App.4th 1510, 1519.)¿ 

  

To establish a triable issue of material fact, the party opposing the motion must produce substantial responsive evidence. (Sangster v. Paetkau (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 151, 166.)¿“If the [opposing party] cannot do so, summary judgment should be granted.” (Avivi v. Centro Medico Urgente Medical Center (2008) 159 Cal.App.4th 463, 467.) 

Discussion

            First Cause of Action for Breach of Express Warranty under Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (d)

            Defendant Ford argues that Plaintiff’s first cause of action for breach of express warranty fails because there is no evidence of a non-conformity in the vehicle that Ford failed to repair after a reasonable number of attempts. Specifically, Defendant contends that Plaintiff presented her vehicle only for basic maintenance and for asymptomatic recall repairs while she still possessed the subject vehicle. On each occasion, the dealership serviced and returned the vehicle to Plaintiff without incident. Defendant argues presentations for only basic maintenance and one- off recalls (to which the subject vehicle did not exhibit the underlying issue) is insufficient as a matter of law to state a claim under the Song Beverly Act. (Silvio v. Ford Motor Co. (2003) 109 Cal. App. 4th 1205, as modified (June 19, 2003).)

Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (d)(2) states that if a “manufacturer or its representative” is unable to service or repair a new motor vehicle to conform to the applicable express warranties “after a reasonable number of attempts,” the manufacturer must promptly replace the new motor vehicle or promptly make restitution to the buyer. (Civ. Code, § 1793.2(d)(2).)

 

In Silvio v. Ford Motor Company, supra, 109 Cal.App.4th at 1208-1209, Plaintiffs presented their Ford Explorer vehicle to an authorized dealer for repair on one occasion after the vehicle suddenly and rapidly accelerated. (Id. at 1207.) Plaintiffs were allegedly informed that their vehicle had no issues but later experienced another episode of sudden acceleration. (Id.) Thereafter, Plaintiffs requested a buyback of the vehicle but were refused and subsequently filed suit against Ford. (Id.) The Court of Appeal found that one instance of presenting the vehicle to Ford was not sufficient for a cause of action under Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (d), as Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (d) required a manufacturer or its representative buyback the vehicle only if it fails to repair the vehicle after a “reasonable number of attempts.” (Id. at 1208-1209.) The Court of Appeal noted that because “attempts” is in the plural, this means a single instance of presenting the vehicle was not sufficient for purposes of this statute. (Id.) 

Defendant presents evidence that Plaintiff presented the Subject Vehicle to Sunrise Ford only on three occasions before trading-in the vehicle on September 16, 2023. On the first occasion, Plaintiff presented the vehicle only for basic maintenance. (UFs 2-3.) On the second occasion, she brought in the Subject Vehicle complaining about the LCD screen glitching, but then declined to have a corresponding software update completed on that occasion. (UFs 4-6.) Then, on the third occasion, a dealership employee came to her home to perform that LCD software update. (UF 7.) In total then, Defendant contends, Plaintiff only gave Ford, via its authorized repair facility Sunrise Ford, one opportunity to repair the LCD screen given she initially declined update on the August 4, 2023 presentation.

However, Defendant’s argument that Plaintiff only gave them one opportunity to repair the screen is unavailing because she had the car serviced twice for the same LCD screen issue. "... [T]he only affirmative step the Act imposes on consumers is to 'permit[] the manufacturer a reasonable opportunity to repair the vehicle.' [] Whether or not the manufacturer's agents choose to take advantage of the opportunity, or are unable despite that opportunity to isolate and make an effort to repair the problem, are matters for which the consumer is not responsible." (Oregel v. Am. Isuzu Motors, Inc. (2001) 90 Cal. App. 4th 1094, 1103–04 (emphasis in original). Indeed, “[e]ach occasion that an opportunity for repairs is provided counts as an attempt…” (Robertson v. Fleetwood Travel Trailers of California, Inc. (2006)¿144 Cal. App. 4th 785, 799.) 

Further, Defendant’s evidence does not show that Plaintiff declined the software update for the LCD screen. In fact, in the cited evidence, Plaintiff told Defendant’s counsel that she did not decline the update. (Plaintiff’s Depo., 36:10-21; 38:12-14.)

In sum, Defendant fails to show that two attempts cannot be a “reasonable number of attempts.” (See Robertson v. Fleetwood Travel Trailers of California, Inc. (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 785, 799 [“The reasonableness of the number of repair attempts is a question of fact to be determined in light of the circumstances, but at a minimum there must be more than one opportunity to fix the nonconformity.”]) Thus, Defendant has not met its burden to show no triable issues of material fact exist and is not entitled to summary adjudication as to the first cause of action.

Second Cause of Action for Breach of Express Warranty under Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (b)

 

Defendant also moves for summary adjudication as to the second cause of action arguing that Plaintiff cannot establish that it took more than 30 days to repair her vehicle.

 

Section 1793.2, subdivision (b) states, in pertinent part: “Where … service or repair of the goods is necessary because they do not conform with the applicable express warranties, service and repair shall be commenced within a reasonable time by the manufacturer or its representative in this state. Unless the buyer agrees in writing to the contrary, the goods shall be serviced or repaired so as to conform to the applicable warranties within 30 days.” These are two separate requirements. (See Cummins, Inc. v. Superior Court (2005) 36 Cal.4th 478, 485 [“Service and repair at the manufacturer's authorized repair facility in the state must be commenced ‘within a reasonable time.’ [Citation.] Goods must be repaired to comply with the warranty within 30 days, unless delay is caused by conditions beyond the control of the manufacturer or its representative. [Citation.]”].) 

Defendant argues the vehicle was only out for servicing for three days between all three repair presentations. (UFs 3, 6, 8.)

However, Plaintiff notes that there are two separate allegations in the second cause of action: that Defendant failed to repair the vehicle within 30 days, and that Defendant failed to commence repairs within a reasonable time. Plaintiff opposes the motion, in part, on the ground that Defendant has only attacked one aspect of the claim, which dooms its motion to failure. 

 

The Court agrees. Defendant is seeking summary adjudication not just on this issue, but on the entire cause of action. As Plaintiff states, the second cause of action contains two claims: that Defendant did not complete repairs within the statutory time, and that Defendant did not commence repairs within a reasonable time. Under the plain language of section 1793.2(b), either claim can be a basis for liability. Defendant completely fails to address this claim. Therefore, Defendant has not met its burden to show no triable issues of material fact exist. Consequently, the burden does not shift to Plaintiff to establish a triable issue of fact.  

 

Third Cause of Action for Breach of Express Warranty under Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (a)(3)

 

Civil Code section1793.2(a)(3) provides, “[e]very manufacturer of consumer goods sold in this state and for which the manufacturer has made an express warranty shall . . . [m]ake available to authorized service and repair facilities sufficient service literature and replacement parts to effect repairs during the express warranty period.”¿ (Civ. Code § 1793.2(a)(3).)¿ 

Defendant contends there is no evidence, or even a factual allegation in the complaint, supporting this claim. The complaint specifically alleges that “in violation of Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (a)(3), Defendant FMC failed to make available to its authorized service and repair facilities sufficient service literature and replacement parts to effect repairs during the express warranty period.” This is sufficient.

Defendant again presents evidence that the Subject Vehicle was presented on only three occasions, and the vehicle was repaired within the same day on each presentation. Defendant argues is no evidence that the servicing dealership, Sunrise Ford, lacked any literature or replacement parts to complete servicing on any of these three occasions.

However, Defendant’s evidence shows that Plaintiff had her car serviced twice for the LCD screen. Thus, Defendant has not met its burden to show no triable issues of material fact exist as to the availability and adequacy of diagnostic literature which was necessary to conduct a proper diagnosis of the vehicle.

 

Fourth Cause of Action for Breach of the Implied Warranty of Merchantability

 

The implied warranty of merchantability is codified at Civil Code section 1791.1, which provides, in part:¿  

 

(a) “Implied warranty of merchantability” or “implied warranty that goods are merchantable” means that the consumer goods meet each of the following:¿ 

 

(1) Pass without objection in the trade under the contract description.¿ 

(2) Are fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are used.¿ 

(3) Are adequately contained, packaged, and labeled.¿ 

(4) Conform to the promises or affirmations of fact made on the container or label.¿ 

¿ 

(Civ. Code §1791.1(a).)¿ Under Civil Code section 1791.1(c), implied warranties have an absolute maximum duration of one year from the sale of new consumer goods.¿ (Atkinson v. Elk Corp. of Texas (2006) 142 Cal.App.4th 212, 230, 231 [expiration is absolute regardless of later discovery].) 

Defendant contends that the only warrantable issue for which Plaintiff presented the Subject Vehicle was an issue with the LCD screen intermittently glitching. (UF 4.) Defendant contends this is an objectively minor issue which did not affect the drivability of the Subject Vehicle.

However, Plaintiff presents evidence that she experienced issues beyond the LCD screen including hesitation on acceleration, loss of power, and hard shifting in August 2023. (Lister Decl. Ex. 1 at 32:19–21, 35:1.) Defendant contends the evidence is Plaintiff’s self-serving deposition testimony which is not corroborated by other evidence. But Defendant fails to explain why Plaintiff’s deposition testimony is not sufficient.

Thus, triable issues of material fact exist.

Defendant argues there also is no evidence of damages in connection with the implied warranty claim. Defendant argues that Plaintiff has offered no evidence that the vehicle was worth less due to any implied warranty issue. But Defendant fails to cite to any evidence. Thus, this argument is unavailing.

Fifth Cause of Action for Negligent Repair

Defendant argues Plaintiff’s fifth cause of action for negligent repair against Sunrise Ford is barred by the economic loss rule.

“In general, there is no recovery in tort for negligently inflicted ‘purely economic losses,’ meaning financial harm unaccompanied by physical or property damage.” (Sheen v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. (2022) 12 Cal.5th 905, 922.)¿ “California Courts define economic loss as ‘damages for inadequate value, costs of repair and replacement of the defective product or consequent loss of profits—without any claim of personal injury or damages to other property.’” (Department of Water & Power v. ABB Power T & D Co. (C.D.Cal. 1995) 902 F.Supp. 1178, 1186, fn. 4.)¿¿

Here, Plaintiff alleges that Defendant performed repair services pursuant to warranty. (Compl., ¶ 15.) Plaintiff admitted in her deposition that she never suffered any personal injury or property damage due to the Subject Vehicle. (UF 11.)

Accordingly, Plaintiff must provide evidence that she suffered a personal injury or damages to property other than Defendant’s alleged failure to repair the Vehicle. Plaintiff does not oppose this point. Thus, Defendant is entitled to summary adjudication as to the fifth cause of action for negligent repair.


Case Number: 24STCV28246    Hearing Date: June 30, 2026    Dept: 731

 

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES

 

DEPARTMENT 731

 

TENTATIVE RULING

 

ENRIQUE MONTELONGO RODRIGUEZ,  

 

                                  Plaintiff, 

   

         v. 

 

 

FCA US, LLC, et al., 

 

                                  Defendants. 

 

 Case No:   24STCV28246

 

 

 

 

 

 Hearing Date:  June 30, 2026

 Calendar Number:  6

 

           

Defendant FCA US, LLC moves to compel Plaintiff Enrique Montelongo Rodriguez’s responses to Requests for Production of Document.

 

Defendant’s motion is DENIED as moot.

 

Defendant’s request for sanctions is DENIED.

 

Background

 

This is a lemon law action. On October 28, 2024, Plaintiff Enrique Montelongo Rodriguez (“Plaintiff”) filed a complaint against Defendant FCA US, LLC (“Defendant”) and Glendale Chrysler Jeep Dodge Ram, alleging causes of action for breach of express warranties, breach of the warranty of merchantability, negligent repair, and fraudulent concealment.

 

On May 18, 2026, Defendant filed this motion to compel Plaintiff’s responses to Request for Production of Documents. On June 16, 2026, Plaintiff filed an Opposition.

No Reply has been filed.

 

Legal Standard

Where there has been no timely response to a demand for the production of documents, the demanding party may seek an order compelling a response.  (Code Civ. Proc. § 2031.300(b).)  Failure to timely respond waives all objections, including privilege and work product.  (Code Civ. Proc. § 2031.300(a).)  Thus, unless the party to whom the demand was directed obtains relief from waiver, he or she cannot raise objections to the documents demanded.  There is no deadline for a motion to compel responses.  Likewise, for failure to respond, the moving party need not attempt to resolve the matter outside court before filing the motion. 

 

            Sanctions

 

Sanctions are also mandatory in connection with motions to compel responses to production of documents against any party, person, or attorney who unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion to compel unless the court “finds that the one subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.”  (Code Civ. Proc. § 2031.300(c).) 

Discussion

On November 14, 2025, Defendant served Plaintiff with Request for Production of Documents, Set One. (Hughes Decl., ¶ 4; Ex. A.) On December 29, 2025, Plaintiff provided unverified responses. (Id., ¶ 5; Ex. B.) On April 22, 2026, Defendant’s counsel sent a meeting and confer correspondence to Plaintiff’s counsel advising them that Plaintiff provided unverified responses. (Id., ¶ 6.)

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that he served verified responses on June 16, 2026, and the late service was due to mistake, inadvertence, or excusable neglect under Code of Civil Procedure section 473. Specifically, the attorneys at Plaintiffs' counsel's firm who were responsible for handling the discovery responses subsequently departed from the firm, and during the ensuing transition, certain case assignments and associated deadlines were inadvertently overlooked and not brought to the attention of the newly assigned handling attorneys.

As responses have been provided, the motion is DENIED as moot.

Defendant seeks sanctions. Plaintiff has provided substantial justification for the failure to provide timely responses. Thus, the request for sanctions is also denied. The Court notes Defendant did not file a Reply to argue otherwise.


Case Number: 25STCV13000    Hearing Date: June 30, 2026    Dept: 731

SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA 

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES 

 

DEPARTMENT 731

 

TENTATIVE RULING 

 

JOHN DOE 1, et al.,  

 

                                  Plaintiffs, 

   

         v. 

 

 

GMRI, INC, et al., 

 

                                  Defendants. 

  

 Case No:  25STCV13000

 

 

 

  

 

 Hearing Date:  June 30, 2026 

 Calendar Number:  9

 

Defendant GMRI, Inc. moves for an order removing Plaintiffs John Doe 1 and John Doe 2’s pseudonyms.

Defendant’s motion to remove Plaintiffs’ pseudonyms is DENIED. Plaintiffs may proceed under the pseudonyms.

Background 

This is an employment action. On May 5, 2025, Plaintiffs John Doe 1 and John Doe 2 (“Plaintiffs”) filed a complaint against Defendants GMRI, Inc. (“Defendant”) and Dujuan Jones, alleging causes of action for: (1) quid pro quo sexual harassment; (2) work environment harassment; (3) failure to prevent harassment, discrimination, or retaliation; (4) sexual battery; (5) intentional infliction of emotional distress; (6) negligent hiring, supervision, or retention; (7) false imprisonment; (8) retaliation; and (9) whistle blower protection.

The complaint alleges that Plaintiffs were employees of Defendant dba Olive Garden Restaurant. Defendant Jones was a General Manager at the Olive Garden restaurant where Plaintiffs worked.

Plaintiffs allege that around April 2023, Defendant Jones began making inappropriate sexual advances towards Plaintiff Doe 1 at work. Plaintiffs allege that Defendant Jones threatened to reduce/cut Plaintiff Doe 1’s days/hours from his schedule if he continued to refuse, which he did.

Plaintiffs allege that in May 2023, Jones told Plaintiff Doe 1 (via translation on his phone) to get in his car or he would be fired. After Plaintiff Doe 1 got in Defendant’s Jones’ car, Jones drove to Griffith Park Ferraro Athletic Fields. Plaintiffs allege that Defendant Jones forced Plaintiff Doe 1 to have sex with him in the public restroom. Plaintiff Doe 1 felt he had no choice, or he would be fired, especially since Defendant Jones had already been reducing/cutting his days/hours from his schedule by this time.

Plaintiffs allege numerous other instances of Jones’ sexual battery on Doe 1.

Plaintiffs allege that in addition to threats about firing and/or reducing/cutting hours/days from his schedule, Defendant Jones threatened to report Plaintiff Doe 1 to immigration if he refused.

Plaintiffs allege that in February 2025, Doe 1 reported the abuse and misconduct to management, but during a meeting two weeks later, management said nothing can be done because Jones no longer worked for Defendant by that time.

Plaintiffs similarly allege that in late 2023/early 2024, Defendant Jones began making inappropriate and flirtatious advances towards Plaintiff Doe 2 at work, and Doe 2 expressed disinterest or ignored such advances.

Plaintiffs also allege instances of sexual battery on Doe 2 by Jones.

Plaintiffs allege that on February 8, 2025, Plaintiff Doe 2 submitted an incident report to management for Defendant regarding Defendant Jones’ sexual harassment and battery. Plaintiffs allege that management said the investigation was done and nothing else.

Plaintiffs allege since reporting Jones’ misconduct their hours/days have been reduced.

On April 30, 2026, Defendant filed this motion to remove Plaintiffs’ pseudonyms. On June 16, 2026, Plaintiffs filed an Opposition. On June 23, 2026, Defendant filed a Reply.

Legal Standard 

 

A request to proceed under a pseudonym is subject to the same analysis as a motion to seal court records. (Roe v. Smith (2025) 116 Cal.App.5th 227, 247-248 (Smith); Department of Fair Employment and Housing v. Superior Court of Santa Clara County (2022) 82 Cal.App.5th 105, 111.)  

 

“Much like closing the courtroom or sealing a court record, allowing a party to litigate anonymously impacts the First Amendment public access right. Before a party to a civil action can be permitted to use a pseudonym, the trial court must conduct a hearing and apply the overriding interest test: A party's request for anonymity should be granted only if the court finds that an overriding interest will likely be prejudiced without use of a pseudonym, and that it is not feasible to protect the interest with less impact on the constitutional right of access. In deciding the issue the court must bear in mind the critical importance of the public’s right to access judicial proceedings. Outside of cases where anonymity is expressly permitted by statute, litigating by pseudonym should occur ‘only in the rarest of circumstances.’” (Department of Fair Employment and Housing, supra, 82 Cal.App.5th at p. 111.)  

 

“Before allowing a party to litigate under a pseudonym, the trial court must expressly find facts establishing an overriding interest that overcomes the right of public access to court records, and find a substantial probability that interest will be prejudiced if a pseudonym is not used.” (Roe, supra, 116 Cal.App.5th at p. 247 [citing Cal. Rules of Court, rule 2.550(d)(1)–(3)].) “The trial court must also find use of the pseudonym is narrowly tailored to serve the overriding interest, and there is no less restrictive means of achieving the overriding interest.” (Ibid. [citing Cal. Rules of Court, rule 2.550(d)(4)–(5)].) “In performing the analysis under California Rules of Court, rule 2.550(d), courts may rely upon factors set forth in relevant federal cases for their persuasive value. What factors are relevant, the weight to which they are entitled, and even which way they cut, may depend on the precise interest and circumstances identified in each case.” (Id., at p. 248.) 

Discussion

Defendant moves for an order removing Plaintiffs’ pseudonyms.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals noted that federal courts have permitted plaintiffs to use pseudonyms in three situations: “(1) when identification creates a risk of retaliatory physical or mental harm; (2) when anonymity is necessary to preserve privacy in a matter of sensitive and highly personal nature; and (3) when the anonymous party is compelled to admit his or her intention to engage in illegal conduct, thereby risking criminal prosecution.” (Does I thru XXIII v. Advanced Textile Corp. (9th Cir. 2000) 214 F.3d 1058, 1068.)
